Microplastics [4848]

By: Carol Albertyn Christie | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Further information:
Microplastics Proposal

Microplastics Ideas

This is Durban Harbour. Kriben (fisherman) has been fishing here since he was a child.
Talk about biggest fish caught, how often he comes to catch fish, does his family survive on the fish.
Is he worried about the pollution in the water? What does he find inside the stomachs of the fish that he catches. (He will have found plastic particles in their stomachs.)

Plastic pollution is a problem in the ocean and by year 2050 there will be more plastic in the ocean than fish. The plastics collect in giant gyres or plastic islands in the oceans and they are great cause for concern. Graphic of plastic ocean gyres. Estimates of size range from 700 hundred thousand square kilometres (about the size of Texas) to more than 15 million square kilometres (0.4% to 8% of the size of the Pacific Ocean), or, in some media reports, up to "twice the size of the continental United States". Tremendous impact of plastic on oceanic life.
(Visuals of turtles with plastic in mouth, seals caught in plastic lines etc)
Gyres

And while the bigger plastics may be the most obvious cause for concern, there is a smaller, more detrimental danger that could affect us all.

Plastics don’t remain big, they are broken down by wave action, UV etc and they become what is called microplastics. This is a term for plastics that are under 5 mm big.

Walking along the coast in Durban, its easy to see the plastic pollution but amongst it are smaller bits of plastic pose a problem.
Visuals of beach and presenter with expert finding the the microplastics.

Dr Deborah Robertson Anderson, Integrated Aquaculturist
Senior Lecturer Marine Biology at UKZN explains what microplastics are.

Why do these small pellets of plastic pose such a problem. Creatures in sea can’t differentiate between food and microplastics and many of smaller creatures are eating microplatics. Apart from the plastic containing toxic chemicals like PCBs, they also absorb chemicals from the water.

Dr Deborah Robertson-Anderson . The micropellets are 1 million times more toxic than surrounding water.

Pellet Watch is an international organisation that has scientifically tested these plastics for chemicals and Durban has one of the highest DDT levels found in microplastics in the world.

Where does the plastic pollution come from? Eighty percent of plastic pollution in the ocean is from land-based sources and this pollution finds its way into the oceans through rivers. The KZN coastline with its high population density and high numbers of rivers is particularly susceptible.
80% of the pollution that comes down the rivers comes from domestic use.
A lot of that plastic pollution comes from synthetic clothes,. The fibres are too small to be cleared from the sewerage system and flow into the oceans. Fibres from waste water of washing machines, are being eaten by small creatures.

Visuals of plankton eating plastic pellets. Smaller creatures eat microplastics, bigger fish eat them and go into cycle of life.
UKZN MACE laboratory. Here we see the innards of fish that were caught in Durban, that they contain plastics. The PHD students here have done experiments which show that the plastics stay 3 times longer in the guts of fish than food does, thereby increasing the time for the chemicals to be absorbed into the body of the fish. Fish from Durban Harbour of 187 fish dissected, 34 % had plastics in them. All 16 species caught contained microplastics

Mussel experiment – how efficient they are at clearing water.
Mussels are placed in murky water filled with plastic microplastics and withing a short time they absorb the plastic into their system and the water looks clear.

Why is plastic such a problem? There have been studies that have linked plastics to endocrine disruptions and cancers. Microplastics get consumed by fish which affect their endocrine and reproductive systems thus impacting overall conservation of aquatic organisms
SOMEONE TO TALK ABOUT HEALTH PROBLEMS OF PLASTIC CHEMICALS.

Dr Brent Newman of UKZN has tested fish in the KZN harbour for contaminants and this is what he found. Extremely high levels of PCBs and DDT in some species of fish.
The smaller fish are eaten by bigger fish and we are in line in the food chain.

PHD student studying links between small fish and in human food chain, same as results that they have obtained in other areas in the world.

A large percentage of microplastics comes from microbeads which are in many beauty products. Some countries in the world have banned the microbead but they are not banned as yet in South Africa. Speak to Unilever.

How to manage the problem. Paddle for the Planet has started an experiment to place booms across some of the Mngeni river to collect the plastic before it reaches the ocean. We will go and see one of these booms and talk to the paddlers who started this initiative.

Press Release:


Microplastics
It’s predicted that by 2050 there will be more plastic in our oceans than marine life. But even more detrimental to fish, humans and the environment are so-called microplastics—tiny but deadly pieces of plastic containing toxic chemicals that end up in fish and ultimately in us. Carte Blanche asks: what are the long term consequences of microplastics on our oceans and our food security?


Script:


Microplastics Script


V/O
This is the idyllic Durban, surf, sun and sea. But strewn on the beach are little shards of plastic that are 1 million times more toxic than the sea water that’s washed them onto the beach .

V/O
Initialy the advent of plastic heralded a new age of consumerism. Its flexibility and affordability ignited a treasure trove of new products accessible to all.

Deborah
“We created plastics in the 1950’s to be a permanent durable product. If you look at advertising from the 1950’s we created a society that is throw away society.”

V/O
But at the time no one thought of the long terms consequences of the proliferation of plastic or the unseen dangers it poses.

Link
“Plastic pollution in our oceans is a major problem, it’s estimated that by the year 2050 there will be more plastics in our seas than marine life.”

V/o
Dr Deborah Robertson-Andersson is a marine biologist and has seen first hand the tragic impact of plastic on marine life. Part of her research work at Cape Town’s Two Oceans Aquarium was in trying to rehabilitate baby loggerhead turtles.

Deborah
“We found that there stomachs were full of blue plastic pieces . The juvenile turtles feed on blue bottles when they float in the ocean and they were mistaking these very tiny pieces of blue plastic for blue bottles and no matter how we tried to rehabilitate the turtles, the damage that was done was too severe and they died.”

V/O
Realising the devastating impact of plastic, Deborah continued her research when she moved to the University of Kwa Zulu Natal and dedicated herself to studying the effects that smaller pieces of plastic WERE having on marine life.

Deborah and Bongani
“We have just seen the wave come up here and we can even see some of the microplastic particles , but also you can see plastic practically everywhere. But this is the plastic that people don’t see but this is the stuff that you are worried about. Yes, this is the stuff. “


Link
“Not all the plastic rubbish that is carried by rivers is deposited on the beach, most of it is swept away by ocean currents that form gyres and the plastic is then concentrated in the sea.”

V/O
There are 5 major gyres in the oceans world wide. The plastic in the North Pacific Gyre is estimated to be bigger than South Africa and in places is nearly 3m deep. Gyre is pronounced gyre with a hard g – can you fix in mix

Marine life, it seems is unable to distinguish between plastic and food.
This albatross chick starved to death because it’s parents thought that all of this plastic was nutritious. Scientists estimate that 99 percent of seabird species could be tainted with plastic by the year 2050.

V/O
Deborah believes that it is not only the bigger pieces of plastic that are harmful but that tiny pieces of plastic called micro plastics, may pose even a greater threat.

Bongani
“Deborah what are microplastics?”

Deborah
“Microplastics are plastic particles that are smaller than 5 mm in length and they can get them from 2 sources either they are manufactured to be that small, like toothpaste and face creams and the second product is from bigger plastic particles that have broken down like this one into smaller and smaller pieces of plastic.”

V/O
The impact of these micro plastics on our marine life IS being studied at the MACE Laboratory at the University of KZN. Deborah and Marine Biologist Gan Moodley are heading up this new field of study.

Gan
“So one of the projects that we have embarked on and completed is looking at the fish guts. and these fish were caught in the Aghulas Current Large marine eco system. On analysis we found that 30% of the fish for each species contained micro plastics in them and interestingly all 16 species had microplastics in their guts. This is irrespective of where the fish fed in the water column . Whether they were surface feeders or mid water feeders they still had microplastics in their guts.”


V/O
To demonstrate how prevalent this is, Marine Biology Student ,Sipho Mkhize disected this fish that was caught in Durban harbour.

Bongani
“So you have taken the stomach from the fish and put it in there?
Sipho
“Yes as you can see on the UV light here, that some of the plastics, they florescewhen you put them under a UV light.”
Bongani

“Oh WOW
That’s the green bit.”
Yip.
Bongani
“That’s quite a lot of it.”
Sipho
“So this is what I was finding on my study”.

Link
A large percentage of microplastics COME from microbeads which can be found in many beauty products . Now many countries around the world have banned the microbead, but it is not banned as yet in South Africa.

V/O
Another source of microplastics IS microfibres that are released from synthetic clothes during wash cycles. These are too small to be retained by the standard filters used at sewage treatment plants and SO flow into rivers and ultimately into the ocean.

V/O
Kaveera Singh, a student at UKZN, found many nylon clothing fibres in the Umgeni river.

Kaveera
“Washing machines are basically graters and when we put our clothes in, these fibres are filling into our systems because the filtration is not as fine.

V/O
These fibres and microplastics are wreaking havoc ON OUR marine life.

The contanimation starts with the most primitive organisims at the base of the food chain. This is a microscopic view of zooplankton eating polystyrene beads seen in green. Here you can see the beads travelling down the oesophagus and into the stomach.

V/O
There are many dire knock on effects in the food chain. Gemma Gerber, a student at UKZN, is studying the impact of microplastics on mussels. Mussels are an important source of food in Kwazulu Natal .

Gemma
“We have seen microplastics malnourish the mussels, the mussels mistake microplastics for food, so instead of getting the nutrients that they need they injest the plastic, they have a false sense of being full , that leads them to being malnourished having reduced survival and reproductive success.”

V/O
The situation is far more deadly, to complicate matters these microplastics ACT like sponges and absorb toxic chemical pollutants from the surrounding water.

Deborah
“Microplastics can concentrate pollutants in the water to a million times higher than the surrounding waters.”

V/O
Their studies have shown that the plastics also stay in A fish’s stomach 3 times longer than food AND some have been shown to move into the tissues and lymphatic system of the fish.
Not only do manufactured plastics release toxic endocrine disruptors but also a host of other contaminants that are dangerous to human health—some of which are carcinogenic.

Bongani
“What chemicals have you found?”

Gan
“There’s an organisation called International Pellet watch and they have done a global survey of the contaminants that adhere to these plastic particles and they found extraordinary high levels of organics for example hch’s and pcb and dtt. These are all nasty chemicals.”

Bongani
“But DDT is meant to be banned?”

Gan
“Not in this country it isn’t.”

V/O
DDT is a highly toxic insecticide used to control malaria in South Africa.

Fish is a valuable food source for many South Africans,
Bull Naicker has been fishing off Durban’s coast for more than 50 years. He hasn’t ever opened up their stomachs to check for plastics, but has other cause for concern.

Bull
“It’s about 6 or 7 years I quit fishing in the harbour. The reason being, I caught some good fish at the harbour but no matter how many times, after gutting you clean and scale it, you take it home, the smell of pollution is still there the diesel and oil smell.”




V/O
Dr Brent Newman is the senior researcher at the CSIR and specialises in environmental toxicology. He conducted an extensive study in Durban Harbour to look at whether the pollutants had entered the food web.

Brent
“We found quite a wide range of contaminants in the fish, these included some metals but also other contaminants like pesticides including DDT and class of chemicals called poly chlorinated biphenyls.”

Bongani
“Obviously some people fish on a recreational basis and some are subsistance fishers, there are variants, but how badly could someone be exposed?”

Brent
“One of the purposes of the project was too look at how many fish people can eat without this adversely affecting their health. For many of the fish we are recommending less than 5 meals a month.”

V/O
The CSIR paper suggests that children and pregnant women restrict their fish intake . This study specifically looks at the Durban Harbour.

Brent
“Fish are really important for a number of reasons, particularily marine fish because they contain very important omega 3 fatty acids .So you don’t want to scare people away from eating fish but we would like to identify systems where there should be some advice on either not catching fish in those systems or limiting the amount of food you eat from those systems.

V/O
These clean up volunteers are trying to prevent more plastics from contaminating the sea . But plastics can take hundreds of years to biodegrade – so it’s not a problem that is going to go away. If anything, the ripple effect will only be amplified..


Bongani
“So what is the impact on the food chain?”

Gan
“When little organisms like your zoo plankton for example take up these little particles laden with these nasty chemicals, they then accumulate in these organisms and in turn those get eaten by smaller fish and those toxicants or pollutants are transferred up the food chain and we have indication that there is a bio magnification effect, so it multiplies along the food chain. So when your larger preditors eat the smaller fish, it gets transferred into the larger preditors.

V/O
This is borne out by polar bears in the arctic that have accumulated high levels of DDTs and PCBs in their system and this is affecting their development and fertility.
As long as we don’t understand long term effects on humans, Deborah believes that we must become proactive in protecting our environment.

Deborah
“My viewpoint is positive, If I look at surveys from 20 years ago we had things like glasses and tin cans and plastic bottles on the beaches. With the programmes like reduce, reuse, recycle, people are becoming more aware of their plastic products. Yes, we can do something about it but I think it’s up to every individual person rather than big organisations.”


Promo 1

V/O
By the year 2050 there will be more plastic in the ocean than marine life.
Larger plastic items break down into so-called microplastics. And, these pose a serious danger to the environment and to you.

“Microplastics can concentrate pollutants in the water up to a million times higher than the surrounding water.” OR On analysis we found that 30% of the fish for each species contained micro plastics in them and interestingly all 16 species had microplastics in their guts.

Promo 2

Microbeads found in beauty products are banned in several countries because they are making their way into the oceans and threatening the well being of our marine life. Scientists estimate that 99 percent of seabird species could be tainted with toxic microplastics by the year 2050.

Promo 3

Tiny Sea creatures are eating polluted tiny bits of plastic. Now alarming new research shows the harmful chemicals they contain are devastating both to bigger marine life and human alike.

Promo 1B

A study at the University of KZN has revealed that toxic microplastics are entering the food chain.
On analysis we found that 30% of the fish for each species contained micro plastics in them and interestingly all 16 species had microplastics in their guts.

V/O These fibres and microplastics are wreaking havoc ON OUR marine life. The contanimation starts with the most primitive organisims at the base of the food chain. This is a microscopic view of zooplankton eating polystyrene beads seen in green. Here you can see the beads travelling down the oesophagus and into the stomach. V/O There are many dire knock on effects in the food chain. Gemma Gerber, a student at UKZN, is studying the impact of microplastics on mussels. Mussels are an important source of food in Kwazulu Natal . Gemma “We have seen microplastics malnourish the mussels, the mussels mistake microplastics for food, so instead of getting the nutrients that they need they injest the plastic, they have a false sense of being full , that leads them to being malnourished having reduced survival and reproductive success.” V/O The situation is far more deadly, to complicate matters these microplastics ACT like sponges and absorb toxic chemical pollutants from the surrounding water. Deborah “Microplastics can concentrate pollutants in the water to a million times higher than the surrounding waters.” V/O Their studies have shown that the plastics also stay in A fish’s stomach 3 times longer than food AND some have been shown to move into the tissues and lymphatic system of the fish. Not only do manufactured plastics release toxic endocrine disruptors but also a host of other contaminants that are dangerous to human health—some of which are carcinogenic. Bongani “What chemicals have you found?” Gan “There’s an organisation called International Pellet watch and they have done a global survey of the contaminants that adhere to these plastic particles and they found extraordinary high levels of organics for example hch’s and pcb and dtt. These are all nasty chemicals.” Bongani “But DDT is meant to be banned?” Gan “Not in this country it isn’t.” V/O DDT is a highly toxic insecticide used to control malaria in South Africa. Fish is a valuable food source for many South Africans, Bull Naicker has been fishing off Durban’s coast for more than 50 years. He hasn’t ever opened up their stomachs to check for plastics, but has other cause for concern. Bull “It’s about 6 or 7 years I quit fishing in the harbour. The reason being, I caught some good fish at the harbour but no matter how many times, after gutting you clean and scale it, you take it home, the smell of pollution is still there the diesel and oil smell.” V/O Dr Brent Newman is the senior researcher at the CSIR and specialises in environmental toxicology. He conducted an extensive study in Durban Harbour to look at whether the pollutants had entered the food web. Brent “We found quite a wide range of contaminants in the fish, these included some metals but also other contaminants like pesticides including DDT and class of chemicals called poly chlorinated biphenyls.” Bongani “Obviously some people fish on a recreational basis and some are subsistance fishers, there are variants, but how badly could someone be exposed?” Brent “One of the purposes of the project was too look at how many fish people can eat without this adversely affecting their health. For many of the fish we are recommending less than 5 meals a month.” V/O The CSIR paper suggests that children and pregnant women restrict their fish intake . This study specifically looks at the Durban Harbour. Brent “Fish are really important for a number of reasons, particularily marine fish because they contain very important omega 3 fatty acids .So you don’t want to scare people away from eating fish but we would like to identify systems where there should be some advice on either not catching fish in those systems or limiting the amount of food you eat from those systems. V/O These clean up volunteers are trying to prevent more plastics from contaminating the sea . But plastics can take hundreds of years to biodegrade – so it’s not a problem that is going to go away. If anything, the ripple effect will only be amplified.. Bongani “So what is the impact on the food chain?” Gan “When little organisms like your zoo plankton for example take up these little particles laden with these nasty chemicals, they then accumulate in these organisms and in turn those get eaten by smaller fish and those toxicants or pollutants are transferred up the food chain and we have indication that there is a bio magnification effect, so it multiplies along the food chain. So when your larger preditors eat the smaller fish, it gets transferred into the larger preditors. V/O This is borne out by polar bears in the arctic that have accumulated high levels of DDTs and PCBs in their system and this is affecting their development and fertility. As long as we don’t understand long term effects on humans, Deborah believes that we must become proactive in protecting our environment. Deborah “My viewpoint is positive, If I look at surveys from 20 years ago we had things like glasses and tin cans and plastic bottles on the beaches. With the programmes like reduce, reuse, recycle, people are becoming more aware of their plastic products. Yes, we can do something about it but I think it’s up to every individual person rather than big organisations.” Promo 1 V/O By the year 2050 there will be more plastic in the ocean than marine life. Larger plastic items break down into so-called microplastics. And, these pose a serious danger to the environment and to you. “Microplastics can concentrate pollutants in the water up to a million times higher than the surrounding water.” OR On analysis we found that 30% of the fish for each species contained micro plastics in them and interestingly all 16 species had microplastics in their guts. Promo 2 Microbeads found in beauty products are banned in several countries because they are making their way into the oceans and threatening the well being of our marine life. Scientists estimate that 99 percent of seabird species could be tainted with toxic microplastics by the year 2050. Promo 3 Tiny Sea creatures are eating polluted tiny bits of plastic. Now alarming new research shows the harmful chemicals they contain are devastating both to bigger marine life and human alike. Promo 1B A study at the University of KZN has revealed that toxic microplastics are entering the food chain. On analysis we found that 30% of the fish for each species contained micro plastics in them and interestingly all 16 species had microplastics in their guts.

metadata.Further information: Microplastics Proposal Microplastics Ideas This is Durban Harbour. Kriben (fisherman) has been fishing here since he was a child. Talk about biggest fish caught, how often he comes to catch fish, does his family survive on the fish. Is he worried about the pollution in the water? What does he find inside the stomachs of the fish that he catches. (He will have found plastic particles in their stomachs.) Plastic pollution is a problem in the ocean and by year 2050 there will be more plastic in the ocean than fish. The plastics collect in giant gyres or plastic islands in the oceans and they are great cause for concern. Graphic of plastic ocean gyres. Estimates of size range from 700 hundred thousand square kilometres (about the size of Texas) to more than 15 million square kilometres (0.4% to 8% of the size of the Pacific Ocean), or, in some media reports, up to "twice the size of the continental United States". Tremendous impact of plastic on oceanic life. (Visuals of turtles with plastic in mouth, seals caught in plastic lines etc) Gyres And while the bigger plastics may be the most obvious cause for concern, there is a smaller, more detrimental danger that could affect us all. Plastics don’t remain big, they are broken down by wave action, UV etc and they become what is called microplastics. This is a term for plastics that are under 5 mm big. Walking along the coast in Durban, its easy to see the plastic pollution but amongst it are smaller bits of plastic pose a problem. Visuals of beach and presenter with expert finding the the microplastics. Dr Deborah Robertson Anderson, Integrated Aquaculturist Senior Lecturer Marine Biology at UKZN explains what microplastics are. Why do these small pellets of plastic pose such a problem. Creatures in sea can’t differentiate between food and microplastics and many of smaller creatures are eating microplatics. Apart from the plastic containing toxic chemicals like PCBs, they also absorb chemicals from the water. Dr Deborah Robertson-Anderson . The micropellets are 1 million times more toxic than surrounding water. Pellet Watch is an international organisation that has scientifically tested these plastics for chemicals and Durban has one of the highest DDT levels found in microplastics in the world. Where does the plastic pollution come from? Eighty percent of plastic pollution in the ocean is from land-based sources and this pollution finds its way into the oceans through rivers. The KZN coastline with its high population density and high numbers of rivers is particularly susceptible. 80% of the pollution that comes down the rivers comes from domestic use. A lot of that plastic pollution comes from synthetic clothes,. The fibres are too small to be cleared from the sewerage system and flow into the oceans. Fibres from waste water of washing machines, are being eaten by small creatures. Visuals of plankton eating plastic pellets. Smaller creatures eat microplastics, bigger fish eat them and go into cycle of life. UKZN MACE laboratory. Here we see the innards of fish that were caught in Durban, that they contain plastics. The PHD students here have done experiments which show that the plastics stay 3 times longer in the guts of fish than food does, thereby increasing the time for the chemicals to be absorbed into the body of the fish. Fish from Durban Harbour of 187 fish dissected, 34 % had plastics in them. All 16 species caught contained microplastics Mussel experiment – how efficient they are at clearing water. Mussels are placed in murky water filled with plastic microplastics and withing a short time they absorb the plastic into their system and the water looks clear. Why is plastic such a problem? There have been studies that have linked plastics to endocrine disruptions and cancers. Microplastics get consumed by fish which affect their endocrine and reproductive systems thus impacting overall conservation of aquatic organisms SOMEONE TO TALK ABOUT HEALTH PROBLEMS OF PLASTIC CHEMICALS. Dr Brent Newman of UKZN has tested fish in the KZN harbour for contaminants and this is what he found. Extremely high levels of PCBs and DDT in some species of fish. The smaller fish are eaten by bigger fish and we are in line in the food chain. PHD student studying links between small fish and in human food chain, same as results that they have obtained in other areas in the world. A large percentage of microplastics comes from microbeads which are in many beauty products. Some countries in the world have banned the microbead but they are not banned as yet in South Africa. Speak to Unilever. How to manage the problem. Paddle for the Planet has started an experiment to place booms across some of the Mngeni river to collect the plastic before it reaches the ocean. We will go and see one of these booms and talk to the paddlers who started this initiative.
